newsitem.title: USA: Dole asks "Where is the outrage in America?".
newsitem.headline: Dole asks "Where is the outrage in America?".

text.p: Asking angrily "Where is the outrage in America?" Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole on Friday unleashed a scathing attack on President Bill Clinton and the national news media.

Dole also asked Reform Party candidate Ross Perot to endorse his candidacy if he did not want Clinton to be re-elected -- his first public comments since his campaign's unsuccessful bid this week to persuade Perot to quit the race.

In a stinging speech, an agitated Dole slammed Clinton for refusing to say he would not pardon individuals connected to Whitewater, saying the president was "sending a signal" to defendants to sit tight until after the election.
He also tried to tie the president directly to the "Filegate" scandal involving improper White House gathering of Republican FBI files.
"Where is the outrage in America? Where is the outrage in America? Where has the media gone in America?" a frowning Dole thundered at a rally in Houston.

"We have the president of the United States sitting down there with 900 FBI files, one might be one of yours ... And then we have the president of the United States who won't say he won't pardon somebody who did business with him and might implicate him later on. Where is the outrage in America?"

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, travelling with Clinton in Georgia, responded, "Bob Dole went negative on Bill Clinton and that didn't work. Now Bob Dole has gone negative on America, and that's not going to work either."

The White House in 1993 and 1994 improperly collected hundreds of FBI background files, most of them on Republicans. The White House removed the political appointee responsible for what it has termed an innocent bureaucratic blunder and an investigation by congressional Republicans has not tied Clinton directly to the scandal.
Later, at a packed stadium at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Dole said Perot ought to support him if he did not want Clinton to stay in the White House.

"I don't like having to run against two people because every vote for Perot is a vote for Bill Clinton and Bill Clinton knows it. I think Ross Perot would know it, if he doesn't want Clinton he ought to say 'Vote for Bob Dole,'" Dole said.

Dole campaign manager Scott Reed travelled to Dallas this week in an effort to persuade Perot to quit the race. But Perot on Thursday called the effort "weird and inconsequential," and vowed to campaign to the end.

Dole's tough talk was the second time in two days he has let loose on voters, the White House and the press. Trailing Clinton by double digits in national polls with only 11 days left until the election, the Kansas Republican appeared exasperated and angry.

In Florida on Thursday, he admitted he was frustrated as he warned voters to "wake up" and vote Clinton out of office. Dole denied any frustration on Friday but said he was bewildered that character did not seem to matter to voters.
"Somebody told me the press reported that Bob Dole was frustrated. I'm not sure I'm frustrated but I don't understand," he said.

He lambasted the press, saying reporters were refusing to report stories critical of Clinton. "We're not going to let the media steal this election. We are going to win this election, the country belongs to the people," he said.

Dole is trying to shore up his political base in the South, normally safe Republican territory. Trailing in national polls by double-digit margins, he must do well in this region if he has any hope of winning the White House.

Dole and Clinton are locked in a tight race in Texas, which has not voted for a Democratic presidential nominee in 20 years. A poll in the Houston Chronicle showed Dole leading Clinton 42 percent to 39 percent, with 10 percent undecided and eight percent for Perot.
